children: By Kim Mackrael

BRUSSELS-Belgium's revelation that it had arrested a Chinese citizen on suspicion of stealing advanced microchip technology is fueling European anxiety about Beijing's trade practices and quest for industrial secrets.

Belgian officials said Monday that in May they had arrested a man, who also holds Belgian citizenship, just before he was due to fly to Beijing. The arrest was part of an investigation into the possible transfer of intellectual property and trade secrets from a Belgian semiconductor company to a Chinese company, prosecutors said.

The detention marks the latest escalation in a long-running battle between China and its Western rivals over technological advances in critical industries such as semiconductors. European intelligence agencies have warned that Chinese entities target Western researchers and companies to gain access to technology its companies can exploit.
U.S. restrictions on selling advanced semiconductor technology to China have helped make that industry a prime target.

European policymakers are already considering new economic-security measures to address concerns about China, said Antonia Hmaidi, program head at the Berlin-based Mercator Institute for China Studies.

The Belgian case on its own is unlikely to change the current trajectory, she said, "but it might be enough to give people who are already pursuing this path the impression that this is the right path."
Representatives from China's embassy to Belgium and its mission to the European Union didn't immediately respond to requests for comment on the arrest.

Belgian prosecutors said the 52-year-old man's arrest was part of an investigation into espionage, participation in a criminal organization, misuse of company assets and the unlawful disclosure of company secrets, the prosecutor's office said. They didn't identify him publicly.
The man held a senior research position at a Belgian semiconductor company called BelGaN before the company's 2024 bankruptcy, prosecutors said.

BelGaN, based in Belgium, specialized in making gallium nitride semiconductors, which allow for higher voltages compared with silicon-based chips. The chips can be used in electric vehicles, but also have aerospace and military applications.
BelGaN bought the Belgian manufacturing site from ON Semiconductor, a U.S.-based multinational.

Chinese companies have tried for at least a decade to acquire European gallium nitride technology. In 2016 a Chinese chip-making company launched a takeover bid for Germany's Aixtron, a specialist in the field selling semiconductors to the U.S. arms industry. The U.S. government blocked the acquisition on national-security grounds.
Belgian officials said the arrested man was working at BelGaN while simultaneously acting as a director at a Chinese company that was established soon after he took up his BelGaN position.
"The investigation may point to the unlawful transfer abroad of specialized intellectual property and trade secrets," prosecutors said in a statement on Monday.
Prosecutors said they are still looking for a second suspect.
The Belgian case isn't the first time Western authorities have raised concerns that China's tech ambitions could harm Western companies.

Belgium's state security service earlier this year described a 'Copy to China' strategy that it said involves investing in Belgian companies to get access to specific technologies and then establishing another company in China to make the same technology on a larger scale.

In a separate case, Dutch semiconductor machine builder ASML in 2022 accused a Chinese company of marketing products that could infringe on its intellectual property rights. The Chinese company was associated with another firm that had previously stolen ASML trade secrets, ASML said at the time.

Beijing is trying to become self-sufficient in everything it needs to assure its economic and military security-including semiconductor technology-said Joris Teer, a policy analyst with the European Union's Institute for Security Studies. He said that has led Beijing to provide huge state support for the sector and to rely on cyber and other forms of espionage.
"If Europe does not radically alter its China, trade, and industrial policies, Beijing's industrialization at the cost of everyone else will only accelerate," Teer said.
